Dreamers and Rule-Breakers · The Romantic Period, about 1820–1900

🗺 Your Treasure Map

Your quest: How did Romantic writers, painters, actors, and dancers put feelings first, and how did women artists break the rules of their time?

Why does this history matter? Art and stories capture the feelings of a time where history books fall short. The paintings, novels, plays, and dances of the 1800s show us what people dreamed about, feared, and fought for, including the women who made great art when the world told them they could not.

Setting the Scene: Head or Heart?

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

Who named it?

German writers like Friedrich Schlegel began using the word Romantic for this new kind of art around 1800.

Trains and clocks

Railways changed how people measured time: before trains, each town kept its own local time, so railway companies had to create standard times.

The Romantic period lasted from about 1820 to 1900, right after the Classical period. Careful: Romantic doesn't just mean love stories! The word comes from romance, the old tales of heroes and adventure from the Middle Ages. Romanticism was a movement in all the arts that valued emotion, imagination, and individuality more than order, balance, and logic.

Head or heart? Classical artists looked at the world like a scientist: calm, balanced, and logical. They spoke to the head. Romantic artists looked at the world through their own feelings. They spoke to the heart.

A world in upheaval

  • Revolutions: the French Revolution (1789) toppled a king, and in 1848 more than 50 revolutions swept across Europe, the year of revolutions. People admired heroes who rose from the people, like Napoleon and Simón Bolívar.
  • The Industrial Revolution brought factories, machines, and railways. Cities grew crowded and polluted, so many Romantic artists turned to nature, the past, and the world of dreams.
  • A growing middle class of merchants, doctors, and lawyers had money to spend on books, paintings, theater tickets, and pianos.

What about women?

Romantic artists praised freedom and the individual, but women had far less freedom than men. Most women could not vote, go to university, or own property once they married. Art schools would not let women study drawing from live models, and the top art school in Paris didn't admit women until 1897. Many women writers published under male pen names so that their work would be taken seriously. Even so, as you'll see in this lesson, women created some of the most important art of the century.

Try it

Classical or Romantic idea?

  1. My feelings and imagination are the best guide.
  2. Look at the world calmly and logically, like a scientist.
  3. Escape the noisy city into nature and dreams.
  4. Admire a hero who rises from the people.

🗺 Stop 2 of 8

Literature: Writers and Dreamers

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

Frankenstein's full title

The novel's full title is Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. Prometheus is a figure from Greek myth who stole fire from the gods.

Overnight fame

Edgar Allan Poe's poem The Raven made him famous almost overnight when it was published in 1845.

Romanticism began in literature. The English poet William Wordsworth wrote that good poetry is "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings." Romantic writers put their own personalities and feelings into their work, and they loved four big themes:

ThemeFamous works
NatureWordsworth's poems about meadows and streams; John Keats, Ode to a Nightingale (1819)
Horror and the supernaturalMary Shelley, Frankenstein (1818); Edgar Allan Poe, The Raven (1845); Goethe's ballad The Erlking
The Middle Ages and adventureWalter Scott, Ivanhoe (1819); Victor Hugo, The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1831)
The lives of poor peopleCharles Dickens, Oliver Twist (1837)

The German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote Faust (Part One, 1808), about a scholar who makes a deal with the devil. It inspired painters, composers, and opera all century long.

Women writers

  • Mary Shelley (1797–1851) began writing Frankenstein when she was only eighteen, during a ghost-story contest with friends. It was first published without her name, and it's often called the first science-fiction novel.
  • The Brontë sisters, Charlotte, Emily, and Anne, published their novels under the male names Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. In 1847, Charlotte's Jane Eyre and Emily's Wuthering Heights became classics.
  • The French novelist Aurore Dudevant wrote under the pen name George Sand and sometimes wore men's clothing so she could move freely around Paris. She was one of the most famous writers in Europe and a close companion of the composer Chopin.
Connection: Romantic artists dreamed of a union of the arts: poets wanted poetry to be musical, and musicians wanted music to be poetic. In Part 2, you'll hear how Goethe's The Erlking became a famous song by Schubert.

Try it

Which Romantic theme?

  1. Frankenstein
  2. Ivanhoe
  3. Ode to a Nightingale
  4. The Raven

Mary Shelley, the Brontës, and George Sand all faced limits because they were women. Why do you think they kept writing anyway? What does that tell you about them?

Visual Art: Painting Feelings

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

A homebody painter

John Constable never traveled outside England. He found everything he wanted to paint near home.

Turner's treasure

Turner left about 300 oil paintings and around 30,000 sketches and watercolors to the British nation.

Romantic painters broke away from the calm, balanced poses of Neoclassical art. They used bolder, more brilliant colors and dramatic motion, and they painted whatever moved them: wild nature, storms at sea, dreams, far-off lands, and the revolutions of their own time.

Caspar David Friedrich (1774–1840), the greatest Romantic painter in Germany, painted landscapes to show feelings. His paintings often include tiny, lonely figures facing huge skies and seas at dawn or twilight. That feeling of awe, wonder, and even fear before the vastness of nature is called the sublime.

In England, John Constable (1776–1837) loved the ordinary countryside. He made sketches outdoors, studying clouds and light, before painting in his studio. The Hay Wain won a gold medal in Paris in 1824.

J. M. W. Turner (1775–1851) painted light and color more than objects. In his storms and sunsets, shapes melt into swirling, glowing color, so some of his late paintings look almost abstract.

In France, Eugène Delacroix (1798–1863) painted emotional scenes from history, literature, and far-off lands, with vivid color and energetic brushwork. He was a close friend of Chopin and painted his portrait.

Connection: Romantic painters and composers wanted the same thing: to make you feel something. Turner's blazing storms are like the rich, colorful sound of the Romantic orchestra you'll hear in Part 2.

Try it

Which painter?

  1. Tiny, lonely figures before a huge twilight sky
  2. Sketches of clouds made outdoors, then a painting of the countryside
  3. Shapes melting into swirling, glowing light and color
  4. A portrait of his friend Chopin

Look closely at one of the three paintings in this room. What feeling does it give you, and which details create that feeling?

Visual Art: Women Artists and the Real World

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

Where to see it

Rosa Bonheur's The Horse Fair hangs today in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York.

An American in Paris

Mary Cassatt was born near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and helped American collectors discover the Impressionists.

In the middle of the 1800s, some artists turned away from Romantic dreams to paint the world as it truly is, especially the lives of ordinary working people. This movement is called Realism. Jean-François Millet painted peasants working the land with quiet dignity, and Gustave Courbet shocked Paris with huge paintings of ordinary townspeople.

Women who broke the rules

  • Rosa Bonheur (1822–1899) was the most famous woman painter of the 1800s, known for her powerful paintings of animals, like The Horse Fair (1852–1855). To study horses and cattle up close at markets, she needed a police permit to wear trousers, because women in Paris were not allowed to wear them in public! In 1865, she became the first woman artist to receive France's highest honor, the Legion of Honor.
  • In 1874, a group of young painters held their own exhibition in Paris, and a critic mocked a painting by Claude Monet called Impression, Sunrise. The name stuck: Impressionism, quick, colorful "impressions" of light and everyday life. Berthe Morisot (1841–1895) was a founding member and showed her work in that very first exhibition.
  • The American Mary Cassatt (1844–1926) joined the Impressionists in Paris. She often painted women and children in tender, everyday moments.
A Louisiana connection: The Impressionist Edgar Degas, a friend of Cassatt, had family in New Orleans: his mother was born there. In 1872 and 1873 he stayed with his relatives and painted A Cotton Office in New Orleans (1873), which became the first of his paintings bought by a museum.

Try it

Who was it?

  1. Needed a police permit to wear trousers while studying animals
  2. A founding member of the Impressionists in 1874
  3. An American who painted women and children
  4. Painted peasant women gleaning grain

🗺 Stop 5 of 8

Theater: Melodrama and Breaking the Rules

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

From stage to screen

Pianists in silent-movie theaters borrowed melodrama's tricks, playing "hurry music" for chases and spooky music for villains.

Another Hugo hit

Victor Hugo also wrote the novel Les Misérables (1862), which became a famous musical in the 1980s.

Melodrama was the most popular kind of theater of the 1800s. The name comes from the Greek melos, "song," plus drama, because music played throughout the play, underscoring the emotions, like a movie soundtrack today.

  • Stock characters: a good hero or heroine, a wicked villain, and a funny sidekick.
  • Poetic justice: in the end, good is rewarded and evil is punished.
  • Spectacle: amazing stage effects for shipwrecks, floods, and even train crashes!

The battle of Hernani (1830)

For more than a century, French plays followed strict rules: a serious play could never mix in comedy, never show violence, and had to take place in one place and in one day. In 1830, the young writer Victor Hugo broke all these rules in his play Hernani. On opening night, Hugo's young supporters and the defenders of the old rules battled in the audience, shouting so loudly that the actors could hardly be heard, and the fight went on for several nights!

Women on stage: Actresses became stars in this century. The Irish actress Harriet Smithson thrilled Paris in 1827 playing Shakespeare's Ophelia and Juliet, and she inspired the composer Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique, which you'll hear in Part 2.
A Louisiana connection: New Orleans was one of America's great theater cities. In 1824, the American Theatre on Camp Street had gas lighting two years before any theater in New York, and in 1835 the St. Charles Theatre opened with the largest stage in the country.

Try it

Melodrama or Hernani?

  1. Music plays throughout, underscoring the emotions
  2. A villain is defeated and the hero is rewarded
  3. Audiences battle in the theater in 1830
  4. A spectacular train crash on stage

Melodrama is still everywhere today. Name a movie or show with a clear hero, a villain, a funny sidekick, and music that tells you how to feel.

Theater: Toward Real Life

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

A different ending

Some theaters in Germany were so upset by A Doll's House that Ibsen was pushed to write an alternate ending where Nora stays.

Comedy or tragedy?

Chekhov insisted that The Cherry Orchard was a comedy, even though many directors staged it as a sad drama.

By the end of the century, many playwrights reacted against melodrama's exaggerated style. They wanted the stage to show life as it really is. This is Realism in theater. Theaters began to use the box set: three walls and a ceiling, like a real room with the fourth wall removed so the audience can look in.

Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) of Norway, the father of modern drama, wrote realistic plays in everyday language. In A Doll's House (1879), a wife named Nora realizes her husband treats her like a doll, not an equal partner, and she leaves to discover who she really is. When she slammed the door at the end, audiences were shocked. The play started arguments all over Europe about the rights of women.

In Russia, Anton Chekhov (1860–1904), who was also a doctor, wrote plays full of everyday moments, where characters don't always say what they feel. The true feelings hidden under the words are called subtext. The director Konstantin Stanislavski trained actors to act naturally, using the "magic if": "What would I do if I were this character?" His system is still used by actors in theater, film, and TV.

In Ireland, Lady Augusta Gregory (1852–1932) helped found the Abbey Theatre in Dublin, which opened in 1904 as Ireland's national theater, celebrating Irish history and folklore. One of her own plays was performed on opening night, and she wrote dozens more.

Theater around the world: Peking Opera

At the same time, Peking Opera took shape in China, beginning in 1790, when performers came to Beijing for the emperor's birthday. It combines singing, acting, dance, and acrobatics on an almost bare stage, where a whip can mean riding a horse. Face paint shows character: red for loyalty, white for cunning. From the late 1700s until the early 1900s, women were banned from the stage, so men played all the female roles. Today, women perform them again.

Try it

Who was it?

  1. Wrote about Nora, who leaves her husband to find herself
  2. A doctor who wrote plays full of subtext
  3. Taught actors the "magic if"
  4. Helped found Ireland's national theater

When Nora leaves at the end of A Doll's House, audiences in 1879 were shocked. Why do you think it upset them so much? How would audiences react today?

Dance: The Age of the Ballerina

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

Darned slippers

Taglioni's pointe shoes were satin slippers, darned with thread at the toes for a little extra support.

Shoes that wear out

Today, a professional ballerina can wear out a pair of pointe shoes in a single performance.

In the Romantic period, ballet became a world of spirits, dreams, and magic, and for the first time the biggest stars were women. Ballerinas began dancing on the very tips of their toes, en pointe, which made them seem to float. Early pointe shoes were soft, with no hard block, so dancers needed very strong feet and ankles.

La Sylphide (1832)

The Italian ballerina Marie Taglioni (1804–1884) became the first great Romantic ballerina in La Sylphide, created by her father in Paris in 1832. A sylph is a magical spirit of the air. Taglioni seemed weightless, and her light, bell-shaped white skirt became the model for the Romantic tutu. Her father made her practice six hours a day for months to master her jumps and pointe work.

Listen to an example

La Sylphide: Marie Taglioni's style. A ballet teacher and dancer show how Taglioni trained her feet and created the floating look of the sylph. Watch for the soft, controlled landings.

Watch on YouTubeBallet Evolved: Marie Taglioni (1804–1884)

The golden age of the ballerina (1830–1850)

StarKnown for
Marie TaglioniA floating, spiritual style in La Sylphide (1832)
Fanny ElsslerFiery character dances from other countries, like the Spanish cachucha
Carlotta GrisiCreating the title role in Giselle (1841)

In Giselle, with music by Adolphe Adam, a village girl dies of a broken heart and becomes one of the Wilis, ghostly spirits of young women who dance in a moonlit forest. In 1845, four star ballerinas, including Taglioni and Grisi, danced together in London in the famous Pas de Quatre. Women ruled the stage, but almost all the choreographers, composers, and theater managers were still men.

Later in the century: The center of ballet moved to Russia, where the choreographer Marius Petipa and the composer Tchaikovsky created Swan Lake (famous version 1895), The Sleeping Beauty (1890), and The Nutcracker (1892).
Connection: Romantic ballet loved the same things as Romantic literature and painting: the supernatural, dreams, and nature. A sylph vanishing in a misty forest is like a scene from a Friedrich painting or a ghost story.

Try it

Which ballerina?

  1. A floating sylph in a bell-shaped white skirt
  2. Fiery Spanish character dances
  3. Created the role of Giselle

Women were the stars of Romantic ballet, but men created most of the dances and ran the theaters. Why do you think that was? Is it different in the arts today?

Connections: Big Ideas Across the Arts

🔍 Hotspots: click to uncover hidden facts

A small world

Many Romantic artists knew each other: Delacroix painted Chopin, and the novelist George Sand was Chopin's close companion.

The same big ideas showed up in every art form at the same time:

Big ideaLiteratureVisual artTheater and dance
Emotion over reasonWordsworth's "overflow of powerful feelings"Friedrich's landscapes of the soulMelodrama's big emotions
Nature and the sublimeKeats's Ode to a NightingaleTurner's storms; Constable's countrysideMoonlit forests in Giselle
The supernatural and dreamsMary Shelley's FrankensteinFriedrich's misty twilightThe sylph in La Sylphide
Breaking the rulesThe Brontës and George Sand behind male pen namesRosa Bonheur's trousers permitHugo's Hernani; Nora's slammed door
Real lifeDickens's Oliver TwistMillet's The Gleaners; Morisot and CassattIbsen and Chekhov's realistic plays

Try it

Which art form shows the idea?

  1. The supernatural: a spirit of the air who seems to float
  2. Breaking the rules: a permit to wear trousers
  3. The supernatural: a science-fiction monster story
  4. Breaking the rules: a wife slams the door and leaves

Choose one woman from this lesson. Explain what she created, what obstacles she faced, and which big Romantic idea her work shows.

Words to Know

Romanticism
A movement in all the arts that valued emotion, imagination, and individuality
Industrial Revolution
The change to factories, machines, and railways that began in Britain
Middle class
Merchants, doctors, lawyers, and other people between the rich nobles and the poor
Pen name
A made-up name an author uses instead of their real name
Union of the arts
The Romantic dream that poetry would be musical and music would be poetic
The sublime
The feeling of awe, wonder, and even fear before the vastness of nature
Landscape
A painting of nature, like the countryside, mountains, or the sea
Realism
A movement in art and theater that showed life as it really is, especially ordinary people
Impressionism
An art movement that painted quick, colorful impressions of light and everyday life
Melodrama
A popular play with music throughout, a hero, a villain, and lots of spectacle
Stock characters
Familiar character types, like the hero, the villain, and the funny sidekick
Poetic justice
An ending where good is rewarded and evil is punished
Box set
A stage set with three walls and a ceiling, like a real room
Subtext
The true feelings hidden under the words
Magic if
Imagining what you would do if you were the character in that situation
Abbey Theatre
Ireland's national theater, which opened in Dublin in 1904
Peking Opera
A Chinese musical theater that combines singing, acting, dance, and acrobatics
En pointe
Dancing on the very tips of the toes
Sylph
A magical spirit of the air
Romantic tutu
A light, bell-shaped white skirt like the one Marie Taglioni wore in La Sylphide
Character dance
A dance in the style of a particular country or people
Wilis
Ghostly spirits of young women in the ballet Giselle
Choreographer
A person who creates the steps and movements of a dance
